cultural.vision_reason: The image shows a strip-woven cotton tobe/boubou robe with checkerboard indigo-and-white pattern and red embroidered neck opening, a classic West African men's garment form consistent with Wolof/wider Senegambian weaving traditions.

physical.title: gown; tobe
physical.summary: Man’s robe (tobe, boubou), tailored from 32 similar strips of handspun indigo and white cotton, hand-woven and hand-sewn together. These would have been cut from a long single strip about 5 inches wide, which alternates rectangular blocks of very dark indigo and white cotton; the weft is of white cotton, but with the occasional use of blue threads to produce a ‘hidden’ weft pattern that enlivens the white areas. Occasional weft patterns have been inserted in the indigo rectangles; these are in most cases lines of red coloured thread replacing the indigo, but are sometimes supplementary weft patterns (these use red, white and blue silk thread). The most prominent of these is inserted in the white rectangle on the back, behind the neck opening. Strips cut from imported red cloth in an S and backward C shape have been sewn down around the neck and over the small breast pocket of the gown; this has a small triangular extension at the top right. The sleeves and the base of the gown have been hemmed by hand, but not lined.
